claims.statement: `DeepAgentRuntime` owns Deep Agents graph construction: it combines filesystem middleware, the built-in clock, conditionally included progress tools, configured runtime tools, optional archive and cron tools, approval tools, subagents, and optional web/help capabilities before the host invokes it through `AgentRequest`.

For each interactive turn, the host supplies request-scoped delivery, tool-approval, and authorization handlers plus trusted metadata; the runtime binds invocation graph, model, approval, history, cron, authorization, and message state in context variables and resets them after invocation.

The CLI creates assistant state and applies retention cleanup, then composes enabled channels and a cron store; model-backed operation opens an optional sandbox plus checkpoint and history resources, wraps the checkpointer in `ConversationSaver`, and constructs the runtime, while an unconfigured model uses `EchoAgentRuntime`.

`TalonHost` starts the runtime before channels and scheduler, unwinds a failed partial startup in reverse order, and on shutdown cancels active work while continuing to stop every managed component even if an earlier stop fails.

Checkpoint and conversation-history storage are independently selected: checkpoint URIs choose a LangGraph saver, whereas history URIs open an assistant-namespaced archive store that is combined with the saver through `ConversationSaver`.

`DEEPAGENTS_TALON_VERBOSITY` accepts only levels 1, 2, and 3; level 1 omits `send_message` from the graph, level 2 enables it with a two-message invocation budget, and level 3 enables it without a fixed budget, while final replies remain separate from interim updates.

Progress delivery is scoped to an individual runtime invocation through context variables: concurrent calls share that invocation's sparse budget, concurrent turns keep separate handlers and budgets, and cleanup restores both bindings even when the invocation fails.

`ProgressMessages` forwards visible main-agent narration before tool execution only when the message has tool calls and does not explicitly call `send_message`; it excludes subagents, while `send_message` uses the request-bound handler and returns sanitized failures rather than transport details.

Tool approvals are persisted as a validated, bounded, non-symlink exact-name mapping with a byte-hash revision; updates are lock-protected compare-and-swap operations, and the approval-management tools expose the invocation snapshot separately from saved changes.

Before an invocation captures its graph, Talon reads the approval snapshot and rebuilds the graph if it changed; construction or policy-read failure leaves the previous graph and active snapshot untouched and blocks that invocation, while running invocations retain their captured graph and policy.

Runtime-tool refresh plus explicit MCP and subagent reload construct a replacement graph under the tools lock before publishing it; a refresh failure retains the previous usable graph, and reloads affect later turns rather than active work.

The host prepares inbound media before building model content; with a remote sandbox, `DeepAgentRuntime` stages documents only after bounded-root, regular-file, non-symlink, and size checks, replaces host aliases with sandbox paths, and marks failed staging as unavailable rather than advertising access.

Inbound documents are represented as untrusted path notices instead of prompt-inlined contents, while eligible images become bounded base64 model blocks; final Markdown image or video references are converted to channel media only when their paths satisfy the configured outbound-root containment checks.

The host records a final reply in conversation history only after successful channel delivery; if a completed turn is superseded, cancelled before delivery, or cannot be delivered, it requeues the background-result IDs carried by `AgentResult` so unreported work can be offered again.

For background-capable runtimes, `TalonHost` runs a post-start dispatcher that waits for an idle, current conversation with pending results, starts a synthetic follow-up turn without interactive authorization or approval handlers, and spaces repeated claims with exponential backoff capped at 60 seconds.

Talon validates assistant IDs, locates each assistant under the configured home root, creates restrictive state directories and defaults, and only installs the default approval policy when `tools.json` is missing.

The checkpoint factory selects built-in SQLite/file, PostgreSQL, or MongoDB support before trusted entry-point plugins; initialization failures are converted to a credential-safe configuration error, while unknown or ambiguous plugin schemes fail configuration.

The CLI exposes `mcp config` and `mcp login <server>` subcommands, and model-backed startup loads MCP tools through `MCPToolProvider`, logging a failed server without preventing construction of the runtime from the provider's available tools.
A background-delivery turn is marked unattended: the host withholds tool-approval and authorization handlers while retaining a request-bound progress handler and the originating reply route.

MCP servers may set boolean `skillOnly`; Talon tags their loaded tools, removes them from the eager graph catalog, and passes them to skill middleware so a matching skill can disclose them when read or pinned, while reload can reclassify tools for an existing conversation's later turn.

`MCPConfigStore` exposes redacted, revisioned configuration management tools that safely read regular non-symlink files and atomically update one validated server under a bounded sidecar lock; stale revisions conflict and a successful write schedules a later reload.

MCP configuration redaction is not a secrecy boundary with Talon's execution-capable default shell backend: absolute-path shell reads and writes bypass the management tools and filesystem-tool permissions do not guard execution, so workspace placement only warrants a warning and real isolation requires a boundary the agent process cannot read.

When an `update_mcp_server` call is not approval-gated and restores a hidden value, Talon rejects any change other than tool filters so a stored credential cannot be silently redirected; this decision uses the invocation's active approval snapshot.

Talon's MCP middleware applies only to marked MCP tools: it normalizes optional empty string arguments, binds the tool-call ID into authorization context, and converts MCP protocol errors to sanitized error tool messages; fresh local subagents install the same middleware.

`MCPToolProvider` serializes refreshes and augments loaded MCP tools with status, reload, redacted configuration, and conditional OAuth-authentication capabilities; successful configuration changes or completed authorization request a reload, while a failed automatic refresh leaves the active runtime graph usable.
